Lecture 15

The algebraic Bethe ansatz

Course map: G2, completed. At one value of the spectral parameter Lecture 14’s transfer matrix is the lattice shift, and its logarithmic derivative is the Hamiltonian. One entry of the monodromy creates magnons, the RTTRTTRTT relation moves the others past it, and the unwanted terms cancel exactly when Lecture 10’s Bethe equations hold. What is left is the eigenvalue of the whole family.

15.1 The question

Lecture 10 found the Heisenberg chain’s eigenstates by guessing a wavefunction, and Lecture 14 showed that its transfer matrices commute. So the question is

how do you diagonalise the transfer matrix without writing a wavefunction?

The answer: the Hamiltonian is in the family (Proposition 15.3); vectors built from one reference state by a creation operator BBB are eigenvectors when the Bethe equations hold (Theorem 15.7 and Corollary 15.9), and the eigenvalue gives the energy and momentum (Proposition 15.10). The worked example is one magnon (15.5).

15.2 The regular point: the shift and the Hamiltonian

At λ=0\lambda=0λ=0 the transfer matrix is the shift

At λ=0\lambda=0λ=0 the Lax operator is a pure swap, Lan(0)=iPan\Lop{an}(0)=\ii P_{an}Lan​(0)=iPan​, and every vertex of the loop turns (Figure 15.1). The state that enters the loop is deposited on site 111, while site 111’s old state is carried along the auxiliary line to site 222; the loop passes each site’s state on to the next, and the trace brings the last one round to site 111.

15.3 The monodromy matrix and its reference state

Lecture 14 built, for the Heisenberg chain of NNN sites, the Lax operator Lan(λ)=λ+iPan\Lop{an}(\lambda)=\lambda+\ii P_{an}Lan​(λ)=λ+iPan​ (14.2), the monodromy matrix and the transfer matrix Ta(λ)=LaN(λ)⋯La1(λ)=(A(λ)B(λ)C(λ)D(λ)) ⁣a,t(λ)=A(λ)+D(λ), \mono_a(\lambda)=\Lop{aN}(\lambda)\cdots\Lop{a1}(\lambda) =\begin{pmatrix}A(\lambda)&B(\lambda)\\ C(\lambda)&D(\lambda)\end{pmatrix}_{\!a}, \qquad \transfer(\lambda)=A(\lambda)+D(\lambda), Ta​(λ)=LaN​(λ)⋯La1​(λ)=(A(λ)C(λ)​B(λ)D(λ)​)a​,t(λ)=A(λ)+D(λ),(15.2) and proved the RTTRTTRTT relation (14.6), Rab(λ−μ)Tb(μ)Ta(λ)=Ta(λ)Tb(μ)Rab(λ−μ)\Rmat_{ab}(\lambda-\mu)\mono_b(\mu)\mono_a(\lambda)=\mono_a(\lambda)\mono_b(\mu)\Rmat_{ab}(\lambda-\mu)Rab​(λ−μ)Tb​(μ)Ta​(λ)=Ta​(λ)Tb​(μ)Rab​(λ−μ) with R(λ)=λ−iP\Rmat(\lambda)=\lambda-\ii PR(λ)=λ−iP, and [t(λ),t(μ)]=0\comm{\transfer(\lambda)}{\transfer(\mu)}=0[t(λ),t(μ)]=0 (Theorem 14.3). The Hamiltonian is H=J2(iddλln⁡t∣0−N)H=\frac J2\big(\ii\frac{\dd}{\dd\lambda}\ln\transfer|_0-N\big)H=2J​(idλd​lnt∣0​−N) and the shift is t(0)=iNU\transfer(0)=\ii^{N}Ut(0)=iNU (Proposition 15.3, Proposition 15.1). The goal is now the spectrum of t(λ)\transfer(\lambda)t(λ): one family of eigenvectors, good for every λ\lambdaλ at once, and with it the spectrum of HHH.

The entries A,B,C,DA,B,C,DA,B,C,D are operators on the chain, and Figure 15.2 says what each does. Read the auxiliary line as carrying a spin from left to right: it enters in the state of the column index and leaves in the state of the row index. At every vertex Lan=λ+iPan\Lop{an}=\lambda+\ii P_{an}Lan​=λ+iPan​ either lets both spins pass or swaps them, so the number of down spins on the auxiliary line and the chain together is conserved: PPP commutes with SzS^{z}Sz of the pair it acts on. Hence AAA and DDD conserve SzS^{z}Sz of the chain, BBB (in ↓\downarrow↓, out ↑\uparrow↑) leaves one more down spin on the chain than it found, and CCC takes one away: [Sz,B(λ)]=−B(λ),[Sz,C(λ)]=C(λ),[Sz,A(λ)]=[Sz,D(λ)]=0. \comm{S^{z}}{B(\lambda)}=-B(\lambda),\qquad \comm{S^{z}}{C(\lambda)}=C(\lambda),\qquad \comm{S^{z}}{A(\lambda)}=\comm{S^{z}}{D(\lambda)}=0 . [Sz,B(λ)]=−B(λ),[Sz,C(λ)]=C(λ),[Sz,A(λ)]=[Sz,D(λ)]=0.(15.3)

The obvious state to start from is the ferromagnetic one, all spins up, ∣0⟩=∣↑↑⋯↑⟩\ket0=\ket{\uparrow\uparrow\cdots\uparrow}∣0⟩=∣↑↑⋯↑⟩, the ∣⇑⟩\ket\Uparrow∣⇑⟩ of Lecture 10. On it every Lax operator is triangular.

Where do the two kinds of term come from? The return is more than a second derivation. Λ\LambdaΛ fixes the eigenvalue of every conserved charge at once — that of dkdλkln⁡t∣0\frac{\dd^{k}}{\dd\lambda^{k}}\ln\transfer|_0dλkdk​lnt∣0​ is dkdλkln⁡Λ∣0\frac{\dd^{k}}{\dd\lambda^{k}}\ln\Lambda|_0dλkdk​lnΛ∣0​ — and the method runs for any model with this R\RmatR-matrix, or the trigonometric one of §15.11, and a reference state that CCC annihilates and on which AAA and DDD act by numbers. That includes chains whose sites carry different spectral parameters; for a larger auxiliary space there is more than one kind of creation operator and the ansatz has to be nested — both are what optional lecture C needs.

15.7 What it buys

  • Lecture 10’s Bethe equations, energy and momentum, a second time, from the monodromy and one reference state (Corollary 15.9 and Proposition 15.10), with the Hamiltonian found in the commuting family (Proposition 15.3). Goal G2 is reached.

  • The eigenvalue Λ(λ)\Lambda(\lambda)Λ(λ) of the whole family, by a method that needs a monodromy obeying RTTRTTRTT and a reference state that CCC annihilates and on which AAA and DDD act by numbers.

15.8 Caveats, in one place

  • Status. Proposition 15.1, Proposition 15.3, Theorem 15.7, Corollary 15.9 and Proposition 15.10 are proved; the proofs of Lemma 15.2, Lemma 15.5 and Lemma 15.8 are readings.

  • The corollary does not say Ψ≠0\Psi\ne0Ψ=0. The singular pair of Lecture 10’s reading, {v1,v2}={0,−i}\{v_1,v_2\}=\{0,-\ii\}{v1​,v2​}={0,−i}, satisfies (15.17) (both sides vanish), and B(0)B(−i)∣0⟩=0B(0)B(-\ii)\ket0=0B(0)B(−i)∣0⟩=0 (the check script, N=4,6,8N=4,6,8N=4,6,8), although neither factor alone kills ∣0⟩\ket0∣0⟩. Lecture 10’s singular eigenstate comes from the regularisation in that lecture, not from the corollary, which is why Proposition 15.10 is stated for regular roots.

  • No converse, and no completeness. That an eigenvector forces the Bethe equations is not proved here, and completeness remains Lecture 10’s cited question.

15.10 Baxter’s T–Q relation

Collect the roots into one polynomial, Q(λ)=∏j=1M(λ−vj). Q(\lambda)=\prod_{j=1}^{M}(\lambda-v_j). Q(λ)=j=1∏M​(λ−vj​).(15.19) Then ∏j(λ−vj∓i)/(λ−vj)=Q(λ∓i)/Q(λ)\prod_j(\lambda-v_j\mp\ii)/(\lambda-v_j)=Q(\lambda\mp\ii)/Q(\lambda)∏j​(λ−vj​∓i)/(λ−vj​)=Q(λ∓i)/Q(λ), and (15.14) is, multiplied out, Λ(λ) Q(λ)=(λ+i)N Q(λ−i)+λN Q(λ+i), \Lambda(\lambda)\,Q(\lambda)=(\lambda+\ii)^{N}\,Q(\lambda-\ii)+\lambda^{N}\,Q(\lambda+\ii), Λ(λ)Q(λ)=(λ+i)NQ(λ−i)+λNQ(λ+i),(15.20) Baxter’s T–Q relation. Baxter found it in 1972 for the eight-vertex model, where the reference-state argument of this lecture does not apply as it stands, by constructing QQQ as an operator commuting with the transfer matrix. It says the same as (15.14), but it turns the Bethe equations into a statement about polynomials.

Proposition 15.11 (The Bethe equations as analyticity). Let v1,…,vMv_1,\dots,v_Mv1​,…,vM​ be pairwise distinct and define Λ\LambdaΛ by (15.20). Then Λ\LambdaΛ is a polynomial if and only if the vjv_jvj​ satisfy (15.17).

Proof. Λ\LambdaΛ is the right side of (15.20) divided by QQQ, whose zeros are simple. It is a polynomial iff the right side vanishes at every vjv_jvj​: (vj+i)NQ(vj−i)+vjNQ(vj+i)=0(v_j+\ii)^{N}Q(v_j-\ii)+v_j^{N}Q(v_j+\ii)=0(vj​+i)NQ(vj​−i)+vjN​Q(vj​+i)=0. So the Bethe equations are the condition that the ansatz produce an eigenvalue of the right kind: the apparent poles of (15.14) at the roots must cancel. For M=1M=1M=1, ΛQ=(λ+i)N(λ−v−i)+λN(λ−v+i)\Lambda Q=(\lambda+\ii)^{N}(\lambda-v-\ii)+\lambda^{N}(\lambda-v+\ii)ΛQ=(λ+i)N(λ−v−i)+λN(λ−v+i) is divisible by λ−v\lambda-vλ−v iff (v+i)N=vN(v+\ii)^{N}=v^{N}(v+i)N=vN, that is eikN=1e^{\ii kN}=1eikN=1 by (15.6): the magnon grid of (10.5).

Figure 15.5 shows both polynomials for two states met in Lecture 10. The zeros of QQQ are the roots; Λ\LambdaΛ, of degree NNN with leading coefficient 222, has its own zeros elsewhere. In Lecture 16 the roots of the ground state fill a line densely and the Bethe equations become an integral equation for their density; Lecture 17’s reading generalises the T–Q relation itself sketched there.

In this form the equations can be asked of any polynomial QQQ, whether or not it comes from a nonzero Bethe vector. The completeness theorem cited in Lecture 10 (Mukhin, Tarasov and Varchenko) is phrased in this language, for polynomial solutions of (15.20) with extra conditions that absorb the singular solutions.

The formulas hold with η\etaη complex, and the regimes of Figure 15.6 differ in where the roots of the ground state lie; for Δ<−1\XXZ<-1Δ<−1 the reference state is a ground state (so is the all-down state). What each regime looks like in the thermodynamic limit is Lecture 16’s business for Δ=1\XXZ=1Δ=1 and is cited here for the rest cited: Franchini, §§4.3–4.5; Takahashi, ch. 4.

15.12 Norms and scalar products

An eigenvector found by the Bethe ansatz comes unnormalised, and any expectation value needs its norm. For the wavefunction of Lecture 10 with real rapidities, normalised by Aid=1A_{\mathrm{id}}=1Aid​=1 in (10.14), the answer is a determinant: ∑x1<⋯<xM∣ψ(x1,…,xM)∣2=det⁡(∂Φj∂kl)j,l=1M,Φj=Nkj+∑l≠jθ2(λj−λl), \sum_{x_1<\dots<x_M}\abs{\psi(x_1,\dots,x_M)}^{2} =\det\Big(\frac{\partial\Phi_j}{\partial k_l}\Big)_{j,l=1}^{M},\qquad \Phi_j=Nk_j+\sum_{l\ne j}\theta_2(\lambda_j-\lambda_l), x1​<⋯<xM​∑​∣ψ(x1​,…,xM​)∣2=det(∂kl​∂Φj​​)j,l=1M​,Φj​=Nkj​+l=j∑​θ2​(λj​−λl​),(15.25) the Jacobian of the Bethe equations in the form (10.20), with each λl\lambda_lλl​ a function of klk_lkl​ cited: Gaudin 1983, proved by Korepin 1982; Korepin, Bogoliubov and Izergin, §§X.1–X.3; the check script verifies it for N=6,7,8N=6,7,8N=6,7,8, M≤4M\le 4M≤4. For M=1M=1M=1 it says ∑x∣eikx∣2=N\sum_x\abs{e^{\ii kx}}^{2}=N∑x​​eikx​2=N. In the rapidities, with FjF_jFj​ the left side of the logarithmic equations (10.18), the same determinant is det⁡(∂Φj∂kl)=∏l(λl2+14) det⁡(∂Fj∂λl),\det\Big(\frac{\partial\Phi_j}{\partial k_l}\Big) =\prod_{l}\Big(\lambda_l^{2}+\tfrac14\Big)\, \det\Big(\frac{\partial F_j}{\partial\lambda_l}\Big),det(∂kl​∂Φj​​)=l∏​(λl2​+41​)det(∂λl​∂Fj​​), because Φj1=Nπ−Fj\Phi^{\vphantom{1}}_j=N\pi-F_jΦj1​=Nπ−Fj​ and dk/dλ=−θ1′(λ)=−4/(1+4λ2)\dd k/\dd\lambda=-\theta_1'(\lambda)=-4/(1+4\lambda^{2})dk/dλ=−θ1′​(λ)=−4/(1+4λ2), and the second matrix is symmetric — the Hessian of a function playing, on the lattice, the part of the convex function of Proposition 11.5. The function whose stationary points are the solutions also measures the size of every Bethe vector.

Real rapidities are a hypothesis, not a convenience. Normalising by Aid=1A_{\mathrm{id}}=1Aid​=1 breaks the symmetry of ψ\psiψ under relabelling the roots unless ∣S(λj−λl)∣=1\abs{S(\lambda_j-\lambda_l)}=1∣S(λj​−λl​)∣=1, while the determinant is symmetric; so no such formula can hold for complex roots in this normalisation. The 222-string of Figure 15.5 is a counterexample: there ∑∣ψ∣2=2.16964…\sum\abs\psi^{2}=2.16964\ldots∑∣ψ∣2=2.16964… and the determinant is 176.2159…176.2159\ldots176.2159…, in the ratio S(λ1−λ2)=0.0123…S(\lambda_1-\lambda_2)=0.0123\ldotsS(λ1​−λ2​)=0.0123… (the check script). For complex roots the determinant needs the conjugation and ordering factors that the bare formula drops; summing ∣ψ∣2\abs\psi^{2}∣ψ∣2 directly of course still works, and the algebraic scalar product below is the systematic route.

Korepin’s proof does that. The relevant object is the algebraic scalar product ⟨0∣ C(u1)⋯C(uM) B(v1)⋯B(vM) ∣0⟩,\langle0|\,C(u_1)\cdots C(u_M)\,B(v_1)\cdots B(v_M)\,\ket0 ,⟨0∣C(u1​)⋯C(uM​)B(v1​)⋯B(vM​)∣0⟩, which the exchange relations for CCC with BBB (more entries of (15.7)) reduce to a sum over partitions of the roots (Korepin, Bogoliubov and Izergin, ch. IX). It is a bilinear pairing, not an inner product: in this course’s conventions it equals (−1)M∥Ψ∥2(-1)^{M}\norm{\Psi}^{2}(−1)M∥Ψ∥2 at coincident real rapidities (the check script), and the sources’ relation C(λˉ)∝B(λ)†C(\bar\lambda)\propto B(\lambda)^{\dagger}C(λˉ)∝B(λ)† belongs to their conventions, not to ours — Lecture 14’s ordering rule once more. The proof itself compares two functions of MMM free parameters. Let the model be deformed so that the two vacuum eigenvalues a(λ),d(λ)a(\lambda),d(\lambda)a(λ),d(λ) are arbitrary, and set zj=i ddλln⁡a(λ)d(λ)∣λj,Kjl=θ2′(λj−λl)=21+(λj−λl)2,z_j=\ii\,\frac{\dd}{\dd\lambda}\ln\frac{a(\lambda)}{d(\lambda)}\Big|_{\lambda_j}, \qquad K_{jl}=\theta_2'(\lambda_j-\lambda_l)=\frac2{1+(\lambda_j-\lambda_l)^{2}} ,zj​=idλd​lnd(λ)a(λ)​​λj​​,Kjl​=θ2′​(λj​−λl​)=1+(λj​−λl​)22​, so that for the chain zj=N/(λj2+14)z_j=N/(\lambda_j^{2}+\tfrac14)zj​=N/(λj2​+41​) and the matrix above is Hjl=δjl(zj−∑m≠jKjm)+(1−δjl)KjlH_{jl}=\delta_{jl}\big(z_j-\sum_{m\ne j}K_{jm}\big)+(1-\delta_{jl})K_{jl}Hjl​=δjl​(zj​−∑m=j​Kjm​)+(1−δjl​)Kjl​. Both the normalised scalar product — the pairing divided by ∏ja(λj)d(λj)∏j≠kf(λj−λk)\prod_ja(\lambda_j)d(\lambda_j)\prod_{j\ne k}f(\lambda_j-\lambda_k)∏j​a(λj​)d(λj​)∏j=k​f(λj​−λk​) — and det⁡H\det HdetH have five properties: they are invariant under exchanging the pairs (zj,λj)(z_j,\lambda_j)(zj​,λj​); linear in each zjz_jzj​; equal to 111 at M=0M=0M=0 and to z1z_1z1​ at M=1M=1M=1; zero when every zjz_jzj​ is zero and M≥1M\ge1M≥1; and their derivative in zMz_MzM​ is the same quantity for the remaining M−1M-1M−1 roots with the modified parameters z~j=zj−KjM\tilde z_j=z_j-K_{jM}z~j​=zj​−KjM​. The modification is the point: ∂z2det⁡H=z1−K12\partial_{z_2}\det H=z_1-K_{12}∂z2​​detH=z1​−K12​, not z1z_1z1​. Two functions with all five agree, by induction on MMM: their difference has zero derivative in every zjz_jzj​, hence is constant, and vanishes at z=0z=0z=0 sketched; the properties and the induction are Korepin, Bogoliubov and Izergin, §§X.2–X.3, in their normalisation.

When one of the two vectors is an eigenvector and the other is not, Slavnov (1989) found the scalar product itself to be a single determinant cited. That formula is the gateway to form factors — matrix elements of SnzS^{z}_nSnz​ and Sn±S^{\pm}_nSn±​ between eigenstates — because the local spin operators can themselves be written through A,B,C,DA,B,C,DA,B,C,D (the quantum inverse problem, Kitanine, Maillet and Terras 1999). Form factors lie beyond this course (Slavnov 2022 is the text).

Summary

  • The regular point (Propositions 15.1 and 15.3): t(0)=iNU\transfer(0)=\ii^{N}Ut(0)=iNU, the cyclic shift, and H=J2(i ddλln⁡t∣0−N)H=\frac J2\big(\ii\,\frac{\dd}{\dd\lambda}\ln\transfer|_0-N\big)H=2J​(idλd​lnt∣0​−N).
  • The reference state (Proposition 15.4): CCC kills it, AAA and DDD act on it by numbers, BBB creates a magnon, and RTTRTTRTT says how AAA and DDD move past BBB (Proposition 15.6).
  • Bethe vectors (Theorem 15.7 and Corollary 15.9): the unwanted terms cancel exactly when the Bethe equations hold, and for regular roots a nonzero Ψ\PsiΨ is an eigenvector of every t(λ)\transfer(\lambda)t(λ).
  • The eigenvalue (Proposition 15.10): Λ\LambdaΛ gives Lecture 10’s energy and momentum.
  • Next: Lecture 16 takes the Bethe equations to N→∞N\to\inftyN→∞.
